title: A Parasite Gives Frogs Extra Legs So Birds Can Catch Them

scenes.text: Some frogs grow six extra legs. Something wants them to.
In the 1990s, schoolchildren in Minnesota found a pond full of them. Extra legs, missing legs, legs that didn't work.
The cause is a flatworm. It starts life inside a pond snail, then swims out and burrows into a tadpole, right where the back legs are about to grow.
Its cysts scramble the growing limb. At some ponds, more than half the young frogs come out deformed.
A frog like that can barely jump or swim. For a heron, it's the easiest meal in the pond.
And inside a bird is where the worm finally breeds. Its eggs drop back into the water, and the snails are waiting.

description:
Some frogs grow up to six extra legs, and a parasite is the reason.
The flatworm Ribeiroia ondatrae moves from pond snails into tadpoles and forms cysts around the developing hind limbs, which can produce extra, missing or misshapen legs; at some ponds more than half of the emerging frogs are affected. Deformed frogs are less able to jump and swim, which makes them easy prey for birds such as herons, the hosts in which the adult worm reproduces.
Which is stranger: the extra legs, or the reason for them?
subject: frog
first_comment: One researcher compared the cyst to a golf ball jammed into the spot where the leg grows. Smartest parasite trick you've heard of?
